question: After a disordered mechanical system is trained to a cyclic limit response at a maximum deformation, can one recover that maximum from global cycle-to-cycle excess mechanical or acoustic dissipation, without observing its microscopic configuration?

key_findings.claim: The crumpled-sheet experiments align one local structural signal and two global excess-dissipation signals at the trained maximum displacement.
key_findings.evidence: The sheet is cycled over [Delta_0, Delta_train] until its force-displacement response and end-of-cycle geometry repeat. During a monotone amplitude readout, the end-state height-map MSE stays near zero below Delta_train and rises above it. In separate global protocols, the difference between the first and second mechanical loop areas and the difference between their squared acoustic signals likewise remain small below training and rise when the previous maximum is first crossed.

anchors.section: Global mechanical signals, Equation 2 and Figure 2
Global acoustic signal, Equation 3 and Figure 3

key_findings.claim: The measured signal is excess dissipation during adaptation, not dissipation itself.
key_findings.evidence: A trained limit cycle can remain hysteretic and dissipate work on every traversal. The proposed mechanical statistic subtracts the second loop from the first at the same amplitude; it approaches zero when the two loops dissipate equal work. The acoustic statistic makes the analogous first-minus-second subtraction. Thus the operational marker is a transient cycle-to-cycle difference caused by entering a new response, not the presence of a nonzero hysteresis area or acoustic emission.

key_findings.claim: The mechanical protocol retrieves the trained displacement sharply in the tested crumpled sheets, but the main paper does not support a calibrated error-rate claim.
key_findings.evidence: For Delta_train=40 mm and N=8 trials, Figure 2(c) shows near-zero mean excess loop area below the normalized threshold and a sharp positive rise above it. The text reports 2 mm retrieval precision and says other train values and readout step sizes were tested. It does not define the threshold estimator, distinguish resolution from statistical precision, give confidence or prediction intervals, report false positives and false negatives, or test blinded unknown values in the five-page source PDF.

key_findings.claim: Transient force-drop statistics support more and larger rearrangements above the remembered maximum only after aggregation, not as a single-readout observable.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2(d) compares pooled force-jump distributions and reports that transient cycles contain more events with larger drops than limit cycles. The paper explicitly says this signal is too weak to extract from a single amplitude sweep and expects larger systems to make it more significant. No classifier, sample count of individual drops, distributional test, or independent held-out sweep is reported in the main PDF.

key_findings.claim: The acoustic readout is an independent threshold signal, but it is not a calibrated measurement of total acoustic energy and agrees only moderately with mechanical excess work.
key_findings.evidence: For Delta_train=70 mm over N=8 trials, Figure 3(b) shows a noisy rise in the integral of B_1(t)^2 minus B_2(t)^2 above the trained amplitude. B is a microphone signal in arbitrary units; the main text gives no microphone transfer function, bandwidth correction, source-distance calibration, or conversion to radiated energy. The acoustic and mechanical statistics have Pearson r=0.65, called weak by the authors, and no confidence interval or event-level causal matching is given.

key_findings.claim: A steel-wool replication shows that the mechanical statistic can work without microscopic access, while also exposing its main confound: slow baseline adaptation.
key_findings.evidence: After 50 training cycles at Delta_train=15 mm, six steel-wool trials show a kink and sharp increase in first-minus-second loop area near the normalized training amplitude. Unlike the crumpled sheet, excess dissipation is already nonzero below the remembered maximum. The authors attribute this to interacting internal degrees of freedom and slow approach to a limit cycle. Therefore, the second material supports portability of the protocol but contradicts a universal near-zero-below/positive-above rule.

key_findings.claim: The shared-hysteron mechanism is physically plausible but not identified by the reported experiments.
key_findings.evidence: The paper argues that localized snapping events change geometry, create force jumps and acoustic pulses, and dissipate work when the previous maximum is crossed; coupled hysterons provide a coarse-grained account. Yet the three crumpled-sheet signals are shown in separate protocols and plots, mechanical and acoustic excess are only r=0.65 correlated, the weak force-event signal needs pooling, and no intervention suppresses snapping while holding other losses fixed. The data are consistent with the proposed mechanism but do not establish that it uniquely causes each macroscopic threshold.

anchors.section: Experimental system and local structural signal

key_findings.claim: The two-cycle subtraction is a compact and valuable measurement design, but its validity depends on a time-scale separation that is not generic.
key_findings.evidence: The first cycle at each new amplitude is treated as the adaptation cycle and the second as the new limit cycle. That removes steady hysteretic loss when convergence is rapid. Creep, fatigue, rate dependence, thermal activation, damage, multi-cycle transients, or measurement drift can instead make consecutive cycles differ below the stored maximum or remain different long after it is crossed. The steel-wool baseline demonstrates this failure mode inside the paper's own evidence.

key_findings.claim: The monotone readout is state-changing, so it retrieves a maximum once rather than non-destructively querying an arbitrary history.
key_findings.evidence: Each readout increases Delta_1. Below Delta_train the end state repeats, but the first cycle above Delta_train causes irreversible transformations and moves the system toward a new limit cycle at the larger amplitude. Later points therefore interrogate an already modified material. The paper studies one scalar memory—the largest prior drive—and does not show that the dissipation protocol preserves that value, separates multiple trained amplitudes, or decodes an unordered sequence.

key_findings.claim: Two frictional, hysteretic specimens do not establish the headline claim that dissipation is a generic memory indicator across driven disordered systems.
key_findings.evidence: The detailed local-to-global evidence comes from unfolded crumpled Mylar. The only cross-material replication is compressed steel wool, another frictional mechanical aggregate with hysteresis, using N=6 and one displayed training displacement. The paper does not test suspensions, emulsions, biological tissues, gels, magnetic systems, thermal glasses, rate sweeps, or a negative-control material that dissipates without encoding a largest-amplitude memory.

anchors.section: Introduction and scope of claimed generality

key_findings.claim: Important robustness evidence is referenced but not available in the canonical arXiv PDF or its source bundle.
key_findings.evidence: Reference note 29 delegates experimental details, error estimation, different training values, readout step sizes, multi-cycle subtraction, and extended measurements to supplementary information, but the printed citation retains a literal '[url]' placeholder. The five-page arXiv v2 PDF contains no supplement, and its official source archive contains the manuscript and four figure PDFs only. The APS record labels supplemental material subscription-required. The main-paper claims can be audited, but those auxiliary robustness claims cannot be checked from the canonical artifact reviewed here.

method.core_idea: Use the extra irreversible work or acoustic emission in the first cycle beyond a trained amplitude, relative to a repeated cycle at that same amplitude, as a global marker of the material's stored maximum deformation.
method.mechanism: Crumpled Mylar is trained by cyclic displacement until its force-displacement loop and end-of-cycle geometry repeat. Readout amplitudes then increase monotonically. A 3D height-map MSE measures irreversible geometry. For global readout, each amplitude is traversed twice: delta W_mech is the difference between the two hysteresis-loop areas, and delta W_acoustic is the time integral of the difference between squared microphone traces. New hysteron-like snapping events above the prior maximum should occur mainly on the first traversal, producing a threshold rise. The mechanical protocol is repeated on compressed steel wool.
assumptions: Training reaches a sufficiently stable limit cycle below the stored maximum.
The first cycle at a novel amplitude contains the relevant irreversible adaptation and the second cycle is already an adequate reference.
Cycle-to-cycle drift from creep, fatigue, rate variation, thermal noise, and sensor drift is small relative to the threshold signal.
Increasing readout amplitude crosses the stored maximum finely enough to localize it before the destructive crossing overwrites the state.
Mechanical loop-area differences and squared microphone-signal differences isolate dissipation from irreversible structural changes rather than unrelated losses.
The crumpled-sheet and steel-wool mechanisms represent a broader class of driven disordered matter.

techniques.role: Drive the specimen repeatedly at a fixed maximum until it approaches a recurrent response that encodes the largest amplitude.
Subtract consecutive cycles at the same amplitude to cancel repeatable hysteretic loss and retain transient adaptation.
Integrate the force difference along the displacement cycle as a global excess-work statistic.
Integrate the first-minus-second squared microphone signal as a second global proxy for irreversible events.
Register 3D height maps and use their area-averaged squared difference as a local ground-truth readout.
Apply the mechanical protocol to steel wool, where local geometry is inaccessible.
Inspect every rendered page, all four multi-panel figures, error bars, force-drop distributions, equations, and references.

evaluations.setting: Crumpled Mylar trained at Delta_train=80 mm, then read with increasing amplitudes and a 3D scan after each cycle.
evaluations.metric: Area-normalized height-map mean squared error against the post-training reference geometry.
evaluations.result: The plotted MSE stays near zero below the normalized training amplitude and rises sharply above it; no aggregate N or calibrated detection error is printed in Figure 1.
evaluations.baseline: Read cycles whose maximum remains below the largest trained displacement.

evaluations.setting: Crumpled Mylar trained at Delta_train=40 mm; two cycles per increasing read amplitude; N=8 trials.
evaluations.result: Mean excess work is near zero below Delta_1/Delta_train=1 and rises sharply above it; the text reports 2 mm precision.
evaluations.baseline: Second cycle over the identical displacement interval, used as the adapted-loop reference.

evaluations.setting: Transient versus limit-cycle force traces in crumpled Mylar, pooled over realizations.
evaluations.metric: Number and probability density of force-jump sizes.
evaluations.result: Transient paths show more events and a heavier large-drop population, but the paper says the difference is too weak for one amplitude sweep.
evaluations.baseline: Force jumps on the immediately repeated limit-cycle path.

evaluations.setting: Crumpled Mylar trained at Delta_train=70 mm; two acoustic traces per increasing read amplitude; N=8 trials.
evaluations.metric: Integral of B_1(t)^2-B_2(t)^2 in arbitrary units and correlation with mechanical excess work.
evaluations.result: The mean statistic is noisy but rises above the trained amplitude; acoustic and mechanical statistics have Pearson r=0.65 without a reported interval.
evaluations.baseline: Acoustic emission from the second traversal of the same interval.

evaluations.setting: Steel wool trained for 50 cycles at Delta_train=15 mm; mechanical readout over N=6 trials.
evaluations.metric: First-minus-second hysteresis-loop work versus normalized read amplitude.
evaluations.result: The mean curve has a kink and steeper rise near the trained amplitude, but retains nonzero excess below it.
evaluations.baseline: Subthreshold read amplitudes in the same slowly converging material.

limitations: Author-stated: force-jump statistics are too weak to identify the memory in a single amplitude sweep.
Author-stated: steel wool has nonzero subthreshold excess dissipation, plausibly because interactions slow convergence to a limit cycle.
Author-stated: the microscopic structure and individual rearrangements in steel wool lie below measurement access or noise.
Reviewer-identified: sample construction, cycling rate, stopping rule, threshold estimator, uncertainty analysis, and robustness measurements are delegated to unavailable supplemental material.
Reviewer-identified: only one detailed specimen class and one closely related frictional aggregate test the claim of generic applicability.
Reviewer-identified: monotone threshold crossing changes the trained state, making the readout destructive above the remembered maximum.
Reviewer-identified: the acoustic statistic is in arbitrary sensor units and is not calibrated to radiated energy.
Reviewer-identified: no raw data, code, preregistered decision rule, blinded recovery, negative material control, or sensitivity/specificity analysis is supplied in the canonical artifact.
failure_modes: A material that creeps or requires many adaptation cycles can produce first-minus-second excess below the stored maximum, yielding a false threshold.
Fatigue, damage, rate-dependent hysteresis, thermal switching, or sensor drift can mimic irreversible novelty during a monotone sweep.
A broad or multi-step transition can make threshold localization depend mainly on readout step size and an analyst-chosen kink criterion.
The first super-threshold cycle overwrites the prior maximum, so repeating or querying the memory in another order may return the readout history instead of the original training history.
Multiple stored amplitudes need not appear in a scalar excess-dissipation curve and may collapse to only the largest threshold.
Continuous plastic flow or absence of a limit cycle can keep excess dissipation nonzero everywhere, even if local configuration memory exists.
Steady dissipation can be large while differential dissipation is zero; interpreting the method as a detector of total dissipation reverses its operational meaning.
Microphone coupling, reflections, bandwidth, and background noise can change the squared-signal difference without a corresponding change in material work.
reusable_insights: Consecutive-cycle subtraction is a low-instrumentation way to separate repeatable hysteresis from transient adaptation when a system converges quickly.
A local structural measure can serve as ground truth for developing a global proxy, but the proxy should later be frozen and tested on specimens with hidden structure.
Threshold protocols should report an explicit estimator, resolution, confidence interval, false-positive rate, and an untouched post-readout check because crossing the threshold changes the system.
Testing a proposed generic signal needs both diverse positive systems and negative controls that dissipate or creep without storing the target memory.
Mechanical and acoustic channels can offer useful redundancy, but only event-aligned measurements and calibrated energy accounting can establish that they observe the same transitions.
The distinction between total loss, differential loss, and irreversible structural work should be maintained when transferring thermodynamic observables into learning or memory language.
open_questions: Can a frozen threshold detector recover an unknown Delta_train with calibrated coverage across many specimens, materials, drive rates, and operators?
Which convergence diagnostic determines how many reference cycles are needed when adaptation lasts more than one cycle?
Can global dissipation resolve multiple nested memories rather than only the largest previous amplitude?
Can one design a nondestructive readout that does not cross and overwrite the stored threshold?
How do thermal noise, cycling frequency, aging, creep, and fatigue change the false-positive and false-negative rates of the differential signal?
Does event-level alignment among 3D snapping, force drops, loop work, and calibrated acoustic energy establish a shared causal mechanism?
What material properties predict when excess dissipation will track a memory boundary and when it will merely track slow relaxation or damage?

competitive_landscape.title: Memory from coupled instabilities in unfolded crumpled sheets
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct prior from the same system
competitive_landscape.difference: Shohat, Hexner, and Lahini establish largest-compression and return-point memory in unfolded crumpled sheets using 3D imaging, global mechanics, and a coupled-instability model. The reviewed paper's substantive addition is a two-cycle mechanical and acoustic readout that aims to work when the local structure cannot be imaged.

competitive_landscape.title: Memory formation in cyclically deformed amorphous solids and sphere assemblies
competitive_landscape.difference: Adhikari and Sastry compare read protocols for single and multiple amplitude memories in simulated amorphous solids and sphere assemblies and distinguish loop from point reversibility. Their observables use configuration changes, whereas Shohat and Lahini target a scalar macroscopic dissipation proxy; the earlier work covers multiple-memory capacity that the proxy does not test.

competitive_landscape.title: Networks and Hierarchies: How Amorphous Materials Learn to Remember
competitive_landscape.difference: Mungan et al. map cyclically deformed amorphous solids to directed transition networks and connect return-point memory to interacting localized rearrangements and one-way transitions. That topology gives a more explicit state-space mechanism; the reviewed experiments infer the same kind of one-way transition from excess work without reconstructing the network.

competitive_landscape.title: Multiple memory formation in glassy landscapes
competitive_landscape.difference: Lindeman and Nagel show that interactions between hysteretic rearranging clusters explain long transients, multi-period orbits, and persistent multiple memories. Shohat and Lahini use interacting hysterons as an interpretation but test a rapidly referenced, largest-amplitude scalar readout rather than those harder dynamical regimes.

competitive_landscape.title: Competition between energy and dynamics in memory formation
competitive_landscape.difference: Hagh et al. show that even one dynamical hysteron can take many cycles to settle and that forcing time scale changes which state is selected. This directly limits the reviewed protocol's assumption that cycle two is a settled reference and shows why a dissipation kink can depend on drive rate rather than only stored amplitude.

competitive_landscape.title: Memory switching due to thermal noise in amorphous solids subject to cyclic shear
competitive_landscape.difference: Majumdar and Regev show that thermal noise can trigger cascades of new plastic events and catastrophic memory loss, with non-Arrhenius temperature dependence and frequency-sensitive survival. The reviewed work is effectively athermal and does not establish how its global excess-dissipation detector separates threshold crossing from noise-triggered escape.

competitive_landscape.title: Aging of amorphous materials under cyclic strain
competitive_landscape.difference: Shohat et al. later measure logarithmic decay of dissipation across three amorphous materials and compare noninteracting, interacting hysteron, and structural bistable-network models. That result broadens dissipation as a probe but also makes age and cycle count explicit state variables that a two-cycle largest-memory readout must control.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Dissipation measured from global mechanical or acoustic observables is a generic, robust indicator of the memory of the largest perturbation in cyclically driven disordered systems.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper introduces a practical first-cycle-minus-reference-cycle readout, links it to a local 3D structural threshold in crumpled Mylar, demonstrates independent mechanical and acoustic curves over eight trials, and transfers the mechanical curve to six steel-wool trials where internal structure is inaccessible.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The clearest novelty is the compact global differential-dissipation protocol and its cross-scale demonstration in one experimentally transparent material plus one opaque aggregate. Largest-amplitude memory, local irreversible readouts, interacting-hysteron mechanisms, and multiple-memory protocols were already established. 'Generic dissipation indicator' is too broad: the statistic is excess adaptation between cycles, its reference assumes fast convergence, the steel-wool baseline already violates the ideal rule, and diverse material and negative controls are absent.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text pass. I read all five pages of arXiv v2 and inspected every rendered page at 105 dpi: the encoding/readout schematics, 3D-difference maps, all axes and error bars in Figures 1-4, force traces and drop distributions, acoustic traces, equations, footnotes, and the complete references. I also downloaded and inspected the official arXiv source bundle; it contains the manuscript and four figure PDFs but no supplement or code. The paper points to supplementary information with an unresolved '[url]' placeholder, while the journal labels that material subscription-required, so claims located only there remain explicitly unverified. I searched primary arXiv and proceedings records using mechanism, task/readout, and claimed-generality query families and checked seven exact competing records and current versions on 2026-08-23. This first pass is not an independent secondary verification.
